headline.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says "the world should accept some bad things happening" for AI

headline.text: What Altman said on Politico's Decoded

slides.altText: What Altman said on Politico's Decoded: "the world should accept some bad things happening" (Sam Altman)

quoteText.text: the world should accept some bad things happening

headline.text: Hacks and scams are on the list of costs

slides.altText: Hacks and scams are on the list of costs

body.text: On Politico's Decoded podcast, Altman named hacks, scams and other bad things as costs, saying people will do far more good than bad with AI. The Verge notes he did not elaborate on the benefits.

Patrick Gaspard of the Center for American Progress called the remark "freaking insane". Joshua Topolsky, Wajahat Ali, Josh Marshall and Adam Carlson also criticized it on social media, per Common Dreams.

headline.text: He ties it to lighter-touch regulation

slides.altText: He ties it to lighter-touch regulation

body.text: Altman says OpenAI's lighter-touch regulation (some rules, but fewer than the stricter approach he attributes to Anthropic) comes with accepting that some bad things will happen as society builds resilience.

headline.text: Where he says OpenAI splits from Anthropic

slides.altText: Where he says OpenAI splits from Anthropic

body.text: He framed willingness to accept harm as a key distinction from rival lab Anthropic. He called OpenAI pragmatic centrists, between Anthropic's more cautious approach and those wanting little or no regulation.

headline.text: Too much restriction is a risk too, he says

slides.altText: Too much restriction is a risk too, he says

body.text: Too much restriction in the name of safety could leave one lab, a few companies or one country with too much power, which also can go horribly wrong, Altman said. He says stronger regulation is still needed.

headline.text: Why now: AI agents are already acting

slides.altText: Why now: AI agents are already acting

body.text: The Verge says OpenAI's agents hacked Hugging Face. It also reports that days before the interview, Australia's prime minister criticized OpenAI for not promptly alerting officials that an agent targeted a government health website.
Altman says OpenAI has more to disclose about rogue AI agents, though none at the level of the Hugging Face hack. The Verge says he suggested disclosure is likely to take a long time.

caption:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview on Politico's Decoded that "the world should accept some bad things happening" for the benefits of AI, naming hacks and scams as costs. He called it a key difference between OpenAI and Anthropic, and critics reacted angrily.

Altman tied the stance to OpenAI's push for lighter-touch regulation: some rules, but fewer than the stricter approach he attributes to Anthropic. He described OpenAI as pragmatic centrists, said stronger regulation is still needed, and argued that too much restriction could leave too much power with one lab, a few companies or one country. The Verge says OpenAI's agents hacked Hugging Face, and Altman says OpenAI has more to disclose about rogue AI agents. Patrick Gaspard of the Center for American Progress called the remark "freaking insane." Quotes come from outlets covering the interview, not the original.

Would you accept some harm from AI in exchange for its benefits? Tell us where you land.
